meta.name: Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival
notes: Festival: Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival (Festival international du court métrage de Clermont-Ferrand), France, organised by Sauve qui peut le court métrage. Editions covered: 39th (2017) to 48th (2026, 30 January - 7 February 2026); edition = year - 1978 (the festival's own numbering of the festival / national competition: 48th edition in 2026, 49th announced for 2027). The international competition has its own numbering (38th in 2026) and the Lab competition too (24th in 2026). The 2027 edition (29 January - 6 February 2027) has not taken place and is not included.

Official website: https://www.clermont-filmfest.org, which now redirects to https://www.lecourt-clermont.org ('Le Court'). The site's section pages (e.g. https://www.lecourt-clermont.org/programmation/selection-officielle/competition-inter/) link to the festival's programme database on Short Film Wire (https://www.shortfilmwire.com/<lang>/<year>/programmation/section/<id>), the film database and Short Film Market platform run by the festival organiser. This database is the only complete official film listing of past editions on the web (the yearly printed catalogues 2010-2026 exist only as flipbooks / e-books) and is used as the primary source for every year.

Primary source: the JSON API behind the Short Film Wire programme pages (https://apifront.shortfilmwire.com/DataServiceRestFull.svc/): festival-programmation/annee/<year> lists the sections of an edition with their screening programmes; films-programme/filter (section, edition, status 'selected') + films-programme/<start>/<count> list the films of a section with original and English titles, directors, production year, main and co-production countries, runtime (seconds), genre and screening programme code (I 1, F 12, L 3 ...); /film/<id>/synopsis gives the English synopsis (the French synopsis is used when no English one is published); film/<id> gives the prizes of winning films. Each film's Official Festival Source is its official page https://www.shortfilmwire.com/en/film/<id>. Country names are the database's English names. Runtime is the database runtime in seconds rounded to the nearest minute (e.g. 25'57" -> 26 minutes).

Cross-check: the number of films per section returned by the filter equals the number of films received for every section and year (adapter check). The 2026 international competition has 64 films, as stated on the festival website's section page ('64 films'). Every included section is extracted completely (all films the official database lists for the section); 'Official Number of Films' is the number of films the official database lists for that year and section.

Every year the official database lists two French films of the National Competition also in the International Competition, without an international screening programme of their own (they are screened in their national programme). This matches the festival's practice of entering a few French films in both competitions; they are kept as rows of both competitions and their Selection Status says so.

Scope (included, in this order): competitions (International, National, Lab; XR Competition 2025-2026), Young Audience Selection ('Enfants' 2017-2025, 'Youth Audience selection' 2026: family and Kids 3+ to 11+ programmes) and School Programme ('A programme for Schools' / 'School Special'), the parallel sections Close-up (Plans rapprochés), African Perspectives (Regards d'Afrique), Pop-Up and XR Panorama, the yearly country Panorama, thematic Retrospectives, Filmmaker Focus programmes, Producer's Carte Blanche, Guest Film School, the special screenings ('Sparks' / Séances spéciales: Decibels!, Thrills, Shorts in History, Ciné-pool, Click for flicks, 3D, Bloody Night, Terror, Trigger Warning, Virtual reality, anniversary programmes ...), the opening-ceremony screenings and the European Short Film Audience Awards programme. Section labels follow the official database; sections whose label changes between years or is missing are given a stable name (e.g. 'Enfants'/'Youth Audience selection' -> 'Young Audience Selection'; the unlabelled 3D programme -> '3D'). Panorama, retrospective, filmmaker-focus, carte-blanche and film-school programmes are named '<type>: <official label>' because their subject changes every year.

Scope (excluded): Audio-description screenings (re-screenings of films from other sections in an audio-described version); Partner programmes (CANAL+, Short with music SACEM, Adami makes its cinema), which are curated by partners; 'Collections' (presentations of partner / archive film collections such as GREC, Agence du court métrage, Euro Connection); the two unclassified 2022-2023 sections 'Michelin' and 'WTF' (no section type in the database); the Short Film Market and its industry programmes (Euro Connection, Talents connexion, market screenings); and the year-round screenings organised outside the festival week (database section types 'In Clermont-Ferrand', 'In the region', 'In France', 'Abroad').

2020: the 42nd edition took place in Clermont-Ferrand as planned (31 January - 8 February 2020), before the COVID-19 lockdowns. 2021: because of the COVID-19 pandemic the 43rd edition (29 January - 6 February 2021) was held online only; the festival editorial in the official database explains that cinemas were closed and the selection chosen by the selection committees was offered online. The official programme of 2021 (competitions, young audience, parallel sections and a reduced set of special programmes; no Panorama, Retrospective or Guest Film School) is recorded as that year's programs.

2024: the festival's XR competition began in 2024 (the official prizes page calls the 2026 one the '3rd XR competition'), but the official database files the 2024 immersive works only as the special screening 'Virtual reality' (programmes VR 1-2, 10 works), without separating competition from non-competitive works; it is kept as one program 'Virtual reality' (the 2024 'Best XR film award by Evaveo' winner is in it). From 2025 the database has separate 'XR Competition' and 'XR Panorama' sections.

Awards: prizes are taken from the official film records (film/<id>, 'Prixs' with prize label and edition) and only those of the edition in question are recorded. Only prizes of the festival's own juries are recorded, i.e. the official juries of each competition, the audience ('jury public') and the student jury, as distinguished on the official prizes page (https://www.lecourt-clermont.org/prix/): Grand Prix, Special Jury Prize, (Special) Mention of the Jury, Audience Award, Student Prize, Special Mention of the Student Jury, Best Animation Film Award, Best European Film Award and the XR competition's Best XR film award. The official prizes page documents the jury of each prize for the current (2026) edition only; it lists the acting prize and the best original music prize (SACEM) as official-jury prizes, so these are recorded for 2026; for 2017-2025 the database labels them as sponsored prizes (ADAMI, SACEM) without naming the jury and they are not recorded. Not recorded (other juries / partners): Canal+ and Canal+/Ciné+ OCS awards, Press Award (Télérama) and press-jury mentions, SACD prizes (best first fiction, French-speaking animation) and SACD-jury mentions, Procirep producer award, Queer métrage prize and mention, Special Effects (Adobe) and Visual Effects (Allegorithmic) awards, Fernand Raynaud comedy award, Festivals Connexion award, documentary prize and its jury mentions, Canal+ Kids / Family prizes, Equality and Diversity award, YouTube award, CNC/Talent scholarship and other grants, Best Photography (Nikon), Click for Flicks (Orange), the unspecified 2017 label 'Award', and European Film Awards nominations/candidacies (not a prize).

When a film listed in two competitions of the same year won a prize, the official record does not say which competition's jury gave it; the prize is recorded on both competition rows with that remark. A prize is never recorded on a non-competitive row of a film that is also in a competition.

Field coverage: titles, directors, countries, runtime and genre (Fiction / Animation / Documentary / Experimental, as classified by the database) come from the official list; a field the official database leaves empty is 'Unknown' (e.g. directors of some archive films and music videos, synopses of most music videos in Decibels!). Language, IMDb links and premiere status are not published by the source and are 'Unknown'. English title = the database's international title when given, otherwise the original title; title prefixes (articles stored separately, e.g. 'Le' + 'Sens des choses') are joined back.

Titles: some official records store the original-script title (Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Pashto ...) in the international-title field and the English title in the original-title field; when the international title has no Latin letter and the original title has, the two are swapped back (e.g. 2021 'The Chicken' / original '鶏'). Titles lost to encoding in the database ('? ?') are ignored. Two films are genuinely titled 'Inconnu' (2019) and 'Unknown' (2020, ArtFX Montpellier); the latter's title coincides with the missing-value marker. 'Jack & Flo' appears twice in the 2025 XR Panorama because the official database lists two separate records (one without director).

No Wikipedia or other supplementary source is used: Wikipedia has no per-edition pages listing the Clermont-Ferrand selections, so every row is official. Raw API responses (trimmed) are cached under data/clermont/raw/official/ so the extraction can be re-run offline.

Premiere status (checked 2026-11-02): Clermont-Ferrand does not publish premiere status. The official film records (Short Film Wire API film/<id>, the festival's programme database; full live record checked for 2026 film 200141283) have no premiere field (the field 'IsPremierFilm' means a debut film, not a premiere, and is not used), the film pages and programme carry no premiere label, and the official submission page (https://www.lecourt-clermont.org/pros/inscrire-un-film/) states that the festival 'ne réclame pas d'exclusivité ou d'avant-première' (requires no exclusivity or premiere). Premiere status is therefore 'Unknown' for all films.

films.syn: Guided expertly by those who live on the land and driven by the pulse of the natural world, Mobilize takes us on an exhilarating journey from the far north to the urban south. Over every landscape, in all conditions, everyday life flows with strength, skill and extreme competence. Hands swiftly thread sinew through snowshoes. Axes expertly peel birch bark to make a canoe. A master paddler navigates icy white waters. In the city, Mohawk ironworkers stroll across steel girders, almost touching the sky, and a young woman asserts her place among the towers. The fearless polar punk rhythms of Tanya Tagaq’s Uja underscore the perpetual negotiation between the modern and traditional by a people always moving forward. Mobilize is part of Souvenir, a four-film series commissioned by the National Film Board of Canada to address Aboriginal identity and representation by reworking material in the NFB’s archives.

films.syn: Évocation de la révolte viticole de 1907 à l'aide de nombreuses scènes de reconstitutions historiques et de document. Cette évocation est encadrée, en ouverture, par des images des grèves de 1947, par des vues stigmatisant la répression et par des plans documentaires d'ouvriers et de paysans au travail tandis que le commentaire appelle à l'unité contre les banquiers, les industriels, le gouvernement et la politique de guerre des « Milliardaires américains». ?Images du quarantenaire des révoltes viticoles, organisé par le parti communiste et mise en valeur de la personne de Raoul Calas, expulsé le 2 décembre 1947 de la Chambre des députés pour avoir exalté la mutinerie des soldats du XVIIéme, alors que les grèves de 1947 étaient à leur paroxysme. Cette évocation historique soignée, fortement marquée par les affrontements contemporains à sa réalisation, montre la volonté du parti communiste d'assumer et d'utiliser tous les grands conflits sociaux antérieurs à sa propre création, ainsi que son désir de s'adresser à la petite paysannerie. La Révolte des gueux fut interdit par la censure.

films.syn: Drew Lord Haig, a washed-up '80s one-hit-wonder turned IT entrepreneur, is stunned when a Belfast battalion invites him to perform at their centenary celebration. Flattered and intrigued, Drew accepts, hoping to relive his glory days and recapture his youth. Launching into his hit single, the audience appear unmoved. But on the opening bars of his long forgotten b-side the brooding, nihilistic Nostalgie de la Boue, something unexpected happens: the crowd erupts. Word for word, they sing with fervor, elevating the moment into something transcendent. Drew is overwhelmed, until, at the bar afterward, he learns the truth: the battalion had adopted his song during the Troubles, using it as a rallying cry for covert, brutal operations. What he once saw as artistic rebellion had become a weapon, a soundtrack to bloodshed. Reeling, Drew returns home, the weight of complicity pressing down. What began as nostalgic curiosity ends in moral reckoning. His music, once his escape, now binds him to a history he never meant to write.
